body.text: Japan-China relations are currently at a difficult juncture. It is all but certain that Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae will travel to China to attend the APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen in November, but the prospects of her actually holding a summit meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping there are vanishingly low.

It is true that there have been incremental signs of a move toward normalization of the relationship: Diet members have visited China, and business groups and economic organizations are gradually managing to make trips there as well. Still, it remains hard to say that the situation has improved much. The Keidanren delegation, for example, had its planned visit cancelled.

It is perhaps significant, then, that in October Takaichi indicated her willingness to accept the 1995 Murayama Statement, which explicitly offered an “apology” for “colonial rule and aggression.” One of the four basic documents between Japan and China — specifically, the 1998 Japan-China Joint Declaration — that form the foundation of Japan-China relations contains language stating that the Japanese side will abide by the Murayama Statement.

As a member of the Diet, Takaichi had long been critical of the Murayama Statement, and in her first year as prime minister she had not explicitly declared that she would accept it, nor had she reaffirmed adherence to the four basic documents. Her October statement, however, confirming that she would indeed accept the Murayama Statement as prime minister represents one piece of the groundwork laid for future acceptance of the four basic documents as a whole.

Has Takaichi’s stance toward China been consistent since she took office as prime minister, or has it evolved? Beijing argues that Takaichi has been actively shifting Japan’s Taiwan policy, but Takaichi maintains that the policy has not changed since 1972. It’s worth taking a look at Takaichi’s policy speeches since she became prime minister. In October 2025, she stated that “in the area surrounding Japan, military developments and other activities of China, North Korea, and Russia — all neighboring countries — are a matter of grave concern,” and went on to say: “With China, an important neighboring country for Japan, it is necessary to establish a constructive and stable bilateral relationship. At the same time, it is also a fact that there are security concerns between our two countries, including those related to economic security. We will comprehensively promote a mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests through continued candid dialogue between the leaders of Japan and China.” Later it was suggested that the phrase “important neighboring country” used here represented a downgrade from “one of our most important bilateral relationships,” the formulation previously applied to Japan-China relations, but at this October stage, China did not raise objections. This policy speech essentially carried forward the formulations accumulated under the Kishida Fumio and Ishiba Shigeru administrations, namely “comprehensively advance a Mutually Beneficial Relationship Based on Common Strategic Interests” and “build a constructive and stable Japan-China relationship,” and it appears China had no strong objections. Immediately after the speech, a Japan-China summit meeting between Takaichi and President Xi Jinping was held in South Korea. Shortly after that, on November 7, China famously reacted sharply to remarks Takaichi made in the Diet, and bilateral relations deteriorated.

On February 20, 2026, fresh from a landslide election victory, Takaichi delivered a policy speech that contained somewhat different language from that October 2025 address. The divergence appeared in the following passage: “China is intensifying its unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion in the East China Sea and South China Sea, while expanding and increasing its military activities around Japan.” On security matters, the language had become somewhat more pointed. On the bilateral relationship itself, however, the speech stated: “It is the consistent policy of the Takaichi Cabinet to comprehensively promote a mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests with China, and to build constructive and stable relations. Precisely because China is an important neighbor and there are various issues and concerns between us, we will continue our communication and respond calmly and appropriately from the perspective of our national interests.” The phrase “it is also a fact that there are security concerns between our two countries” had disappeared, replaced by “various issues and concerns,” and “continued candid dialogue between the leaders of Japan and China” had given way to “continue our communication.” This presumably reflected the deterioration in the relationship. Yet the formulations “comprehensively advance a Mutually Beneficial Relationship Based on Common Strategic Interests” and “build a constructive and stable Japan-China relationship” were retained.

Now consider the policy speech Takaichi delivered after her October 2026 cabinet reshuffle. Here, the language on security has undergone significant change. Phrases such as “Japan’s security environment is changing at an accelerating pace and becoming increasingly complex and severe” appear, while direct references to China disappear. On the bilateral relationship, the speech stated: “China is an important neighbor, and despite challenges in our relationship, ties between our two countries have been built up over many years.” The phrase “over many years” was newly inserted. Furthermore, language such as “with regard to various issues in the East and South China Seas, military activities around Japan, coercive measures, the safety of Japanese nationals, and human rights concerns, we will clearly assert Japan’s positions where they need to be asserted, and strongly urge China to act responsibly” has been added, incorporating security concerns and related matters. And with “we will maintain communication about common challenges, promote dialogue to protect Japan’s national interests, and work to build a constructive and stable Japan-China relationship,” the Japanese prime minister is sending a message making “common challenges” the basis of the relationship. Yet here too, the formulations “comprehensively advance a Mutually Beneficial Relationship Based on Common Strategic Interests” and “build a constructive and stable Japan-China relationship” have been retained.

Thus, Takaichi administration China policy has been consistent in two respects: the commitment to “comprehensively advance a Mutually Beneficial Relationship Based on Common Strategic Interests” and “build a constructive and stable Japan-China relationship,” together with the emphasis on security concerns. Yet the October 2026 speech in particular saw the new insertion of language — “over many years” and “common challenges” — that can also be read as messaging to encourage dialogue.

Beijing criticizes the Takaichi administration as neo-militarist. Yet the messages sent toward China from the Takaichi administration are neither aggressive nor hardened. Certainly, given that domestic conservatives form her support base, she does make reference to security concerns vis-à-vis China. But we must not forget that she has also been sending messages (incrementally, to be sure) that encourage dialogue. In fact, domestic Japanese opinion polls show that a majority of Japanese now favor dialogue with China.

The problem, however, is time. China’s political personnel season ahead of the autumn 2027 party congress is about to intensify. The closer it gets to autumn 2027, the more difficult it will become to shift the trajectory of Japan-China relations. Japan will continue its efforts to find footholds for dialogue with China, while reading the trajectory of U.S.-China relations and gauging domestic public opinion.
